articles.title: Emergency doctor 'completely terrified' of looming winter pressures on NHS
articles.summary: Dr Fiona Hunter says A&E departments are providing "unsafe" levels of care, with some patients spending 72 hours on trolleys in hospital corridors.
articles.body:
A leading emergency doctor has said she is "completely terrified" about upcoming winter pressures on Scotland's already-stretched NHS.

Dr Fiona Hunter, vice chair of the Royal College of Emergency Medicine Scotland, said A&E departments were providing "unsafe" levels of care, with some patients spending 72 hours on trolleys in hospital corridors.

Although Health Secretary Angela Constance vowed in August to "eradicate" corridor care, Hunter told BBC Scotland's The Sunday Show there had been a "toxic normalisation" of this practice which can lead to patients dying.

Constance told the programme that the winter would be "difficult" but reiterated that corridor care was unacceptable.

She said her priorities were to reduce avoidable hospital admissions, including with "robust" public messaging, to ensure people were accessing the right sort of medical care.

She said she wanted to remedy a lack of statistics kept around corridor care and to move towards a system where preparing for winter was a "year-round" activity.

BBC Scotland has asked the Scottish government for a response to Hunter's comments, which were broadcast after the health secretary's interview.

Last month First Minister John Swinney confirmed plans to cut the number of mainland health boards from 11 to two in a bid to free up more time and capacity for treatment.

But with major reform some way off, fears are growing about the months ahead.

Asked how concerned she was, Hunter said: "Completely terrified, to be clear about the situation currently, before we get into proper winter where the viruses really hit.

"We are providing unsafe levels of care in emergency departments.

"There has been a real toxic normalisation of corridor care. We accept it on a daily basis.

"You come into a department that is completely stacked with ambulances outside and we have got trolleys up and down corridors."

She added trolley mattresses were designed to keep patients for up to four hours but some are being kept for "up to three days".

Hunter said: "We know that excess mortality happens when you languish on a hospital trolley."

The doctor said she did not want to "scare patients away" from coming to an emergency department.

However, she warned: "We are not able to provide safe levels of care because what emergency staff are being asked to do across the country is to look after essentially a ward's worth of extra patients and keep seeing every patient that comes through the front door.

"Some departments across the UK are working at 500% capacity but they don't have 500% extra staff to deal with that.

"So we have really high rates of sickness and burnout among staff - and this is before the viruses really hit."

She told the programme staff naturally want to isolate sick patients but were unable to do so due to "completely stowed out" waiting rooms.

The medic said that, month-on-month, almost 2,000 patients were experiencing delayed discharge across the country.

She said: "If we could free up a quarter of those patients then we would have flow to bring our patients through the system."

Has Scotland's NHS recovered from the Covid pandemic?

Will walk-in GP clinics deliver one million extra appointments?

Councillor Paul Kelly, Cosla spokesman for health and social care, agreed the problems facing the NHS now amount to a "year-round crisis".

He told the programme: "Like everybody we are very worried about what the winter will bring."

Asked about the additional time some people are spending in hospital, Kelly said: "Delayed discharged is a significant problem, as is people waiting for a care package in the community.

"We are very, very clear to the government that we need to see investment in social care."

The health secretary earlier told the programme that there should not be a focus on outcomes, not just money.

But Kelly responded: "I think we have to focus on the money.

"If we are saying the government are focusing on delayed discharge then part of that is about the role of councils and supporting people to get out of hospital."

He told the The Sunday Show that health and social care partnerships currently had "almost half a billion pounds of a budget gap" but added it was vital to invest in the workforce.

Kelly said "urgent" investment was required and added: "We don't want to see anybody in hospital longer than they should be."

Earlier, the health secretary was asked about the outlook for the coming months.

Constance said: "We do know that the winter will be difficult.

"There are always increased pressures as we enter the winter season but what we have seen in Scotland, over the past few years, is an increase in demand on our NHS services."

The minister said a range of factors were responsible but added the government was aiming to reduced "avoidable hospital admissions".

She also stressed the importance of the public choosing the right service for advice and treatment.

Challenged on lack of capacity, Constance said: "We are supportive, both financially and in terms of a policy perspective, of being able to get, what they call, a better flow through the hospital when people have to be admitted."

The health secretary was also asked if treating patients in corridors was "becoming the norm".

She said: "We cannot accept corridor care."

The minister said the problem was particularity acute in certain hospitals and parts of the country.

Asked about concerns delays were costing lives, Constance said: "Our NHS is safe but we need to be sure that people get the right care at the right time."

articles.title: At least 109 dead, over 100 missing as migrant boat capsizes off Djibouti
articles.summary: Search and rescue operations conducted after vessel carrying more than 300 people capsizes near Guhere.
articles.body:
At least 109 people, including 15 children, have died and more than 116 are missing after a boat capsized off the coast of Djibouti, according to the United Nations migration agency.

In a statement on Sunday, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) quoted survivors as saying that the incident happened near Guhere off Djibouti’s eastern coast facing the Gulf of Aden and the Bab al-Mandeb strait from Thursday night to before dawn on Friday.

The boat was heading from Djibouti to Yemen with more than 300 people on board. More than 80 people – all Ethiopians – survived the shipwreck while Djiboutian search and rescue operations continued.

“Our teams are on the ground alongside local authorities to provide emergency assistance,” IOM Chief of Mission in Djibouti Alexandre Coissac said, lamenting the “devastating loss of life”.

“This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities.”

Crossing Bab al-Mandeb, a waterway that measures just 20km (12.4 miles) at its narrowest points between Djibouti and Yemen, is a popular but dangerous route for thousands of migrants from the Horn of Africa.

Many embark on this journey in search of employment and safety in Gulf countries, undeterred by the rising instability in the region due to the US-Israel war on Iran and the resumption of fighting in Yemen between government forces and Houthi fighters last month.

The IOM said it had recorded “more than 20,000 incoming movements to Djibouti from Ethiopia” since September 10. Last year, more than half a million people tried to move along this route into Yemen, and at least 900 people died or are missing, according to the agency.

Djibouti is not only a place where migrants depart from, but several thousand people are also fleeing to the country from Yemen due to the renewed conflict.

articles.title: MARC SIEGEL: Russia's mysterious lab death exposes a danger the world isn't ready for
articles.summary: A Russian lab worker's mysterious pneumonia death raises urgent questions about plague, bioengineering and the lack of global health surveillance.
articles.body: Plague is an ancient scourge, and fear of the plague is buried deep in our unconscious. The Black Death caused over 100 million deaths in the 14th century, six centuries before the advent of antibiotics. Compare that to 50 to 100 million deaths from the Spanish flu in 1918 or over 15 million deaths from COVID. On top of severe illness and death, these devastating pandemics have caused worldwide fear and panic. Flash forward six years from the origins of COVID, and once again we learn of a mysterious pneumonia death of a scientist, this time a laboratory worker, Darya Shipilova, who was working in a lab in Siberia that has been studying dangerous pathogens, including the plague. Once again, as with COVID, there are far more questions than answers. Is the pathogen pneumonic plague? The Russians deny it. Has it been bioengineered to make it more resistant to antibiotics and more easily transmissible through the air? The Russian health authorities deny it. Have hundreds of patients been isolated and several hospitals been shut down out of an abundance of caution, as the health authorities there would have you believe, or is this something far worse, as it was during the initial Wuhan lockdown for COVID? Russia is now saying that it is winding down precautionary measures, but why were these extensive measures necessary in the first place? MYSTERY DEATH AT RUSSIAN PLAGUE LAB TRIGGERS SWEEPING PRECAUTIONS AS US WATCHES CLOSELY We may never have the answers to any of these questions, but unfortunately, they not only bring back bad memories of COVID, but they also unmask a continuing lack of a comprehensive global health surveillance network to protect us. The assertions and gesticulations by WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus at press conferences are no more reassuring now than they were back then. US, WHO REQUEST DETAILS FROM RUSSIA AMID REPORTS OF SECOND PNEUMONIA CASE The treatment for these scourges, both ancient and modern, for both fear and the actual disease, as I write in my new book, "The Angels Among Us," is messengers from God to reassure us, treat us, and guide us through, just as Dr. Stephen Kornfeld recently did on the hantavirus ship, the MV Hondius, when another scary disease, the Andes strain of hantavirus, emerged. In fact, fear of an unknown pathogen sparking a global pandemic was the motivation for an international call for a global network of scientists to protect us more than two decades ago. Unfortunately, that so-called network failed miserably with COVID, as China’s smokescreen was famously amplified by the WHO’s declaration in January 2020 that this was only a regional problem. COVID whistleblower ophthalmologist Li Wenliang, who died in a Wuhan hospital from COVID in February 2020 after a middle-of-the-night visit from the police to shut him down, is buried deep in the public consciousness. So, too, are all our friends and patients who died unceremoniously in the first several months of the pandemic. CAN FAITH HELP PATIENTS HEAL? VETERAN DOCTOR REVEALS WHAT HE'S WITNESSED FIRSTHAND One who didn’t die, as described in "The Angels Among Us," was Evie Rodriguez, who was saved not by medicines but by prayer. She was in the ICU at UC Davis, not responding to steroids or a new antiviral treatment (remdesivir), but rather than be overcome by fear, she turned to prayer and was visited by angels sent to her by her father, Pastor Sam Rodriguez. This gave her the strength she needed to fight off the angel of death. "I am fully awake, and a dark spirit with an open mouth comes into the room, and I can feel that it has come for me. To take me. It is very heavy and real, a dark force. I feel it is the spirit of death. I am not afraid. I become angry and demand it to leave. ‘What are you doing here?’ I yell. ‘Get away!’ And it goes away. I will it away." So the risk beyond that initial case would appear to be very, very small. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP But the fear and the global vulnerability remain. Laboratory accidents occur all the time. And we are not prepared for them, especially when it comes to dangerous pathogens from dangerous places. articles.title: Hunters say harvesting their own food deepens important connection to God
articles.summary: Chad and James Hampton spend hours in a Michigan tree stand each hunting season, filling freezers with venison as an expression of Christian faith.
articles.body: For twin brothers Chad and James Hampton, putting food on the table can begin hours earlier — sitting quietly in a Michigan tree stand. The pastors, authors and avid outdoorsmen harvest several deer during hunting season each year, filling their freezers with venison to be eaten. But to the brothers, harvesting their own food represents more than providing meals for their families. It's also intertwined with their Christian faith. 'MEATEATER' HOST SAYS WILD GAME IS 'THE HEALTHIEST FOOD' AMERICANS CAN EAT "We know that God's given us that food to manage and also consume so that we can be what He's created us to be," Chad Hampton told Fox News Digital. The Hamptons, founders of Huntin' the Truth Ministries and hosts of the outdoor show "Twin Factor," point to Genesis 1:26 when explaining their view of hunters as stewards of God's creation. "We're managing God's creation that He gave to us," Chad Hampton said. The connection between faith, food and the outdoors also appears in their new book, "100 Days of Strength for Hunters," a devotional designed to help outdoorsmen strengthen their relationship with God. COWBOY CHEF SAYS AMERICANS ARE TURNING TO ONE OF THE 'HEALTHIEST MEATS,' AND IT'S AT MOST GROCERY STORES The brothers said the book combines Scripture, hunting stories, practical applications and prayer — and is short enough for hunters to take with them into the tree stand. Their approach to food also overlaps with a larger national conversation about eating "real food" and knowing where food comes from, themes that have been promoted by the Make America Healthy Again movement. It's a message that resonates with the Hamptons. "Everything that we harvest we eat," James Hampton said. They also believe many Americans have become disconnected from their food as convenience increasingly shapes what people eat. "We have to live what we preach." The Hamptons readily acknowledge they aren't immune to eating fast food, pointing to their busy schedules. "Although we love our fast food, we also love the slow-cooked venison," Chad Hampton said. articles.title: Sweet protein brazzein shows promise in reducing blood sugar spikes: Study
articles.summary: Russian research reveals that the protein brazzein could help reduce blood sugar spikes.
articles.body:
A new study has shown how the sweet protein brazzein could help reduce blood sugar spikes, the Science Alert news outlet reported.

Brazzein is a natural protein originally found in the West African oubli plant, but now largely produced through a fermentation process. It is known for its intense sweetness and has long been eyed as a potential sugar alternative.

Researchers at Russia’s Federal Research Centre of Nutrition, Biotechnology and Food Safety conducted a test on 101 adults living with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). The condition, where fat builds up in the liver, is often associated with diabetes and obesity.

The study, published in the Clinical Nutrition ESPEN journal, was a randomised trial that focused on ice cream.

Participants ate a 100 gram vanilla ice cream serving on three separate days: one with sugar, one with brazzein, and one day with brazzein and a fibre called inulin.

Post-meal blood sugar spikes were lower when participants consumed the brazzein or brazzein and inulin versions, compared with the sugar-sweetened version, the study showed.

The reductions in sugar spikes were most notable in participants with type 2 diabetes, according to the study.

“Longer-term studies are needed to determine whether repeated substitution of sucrose-containing desserts with brazzein-sweetened alternatives translates into sustained metabolic, hepatic, microbiome, or behavioural benefits,” the researchers wrote.

The negative health effects of sugar have been widely researched and debated over the years.

The World Health Organization advised in 2023 against the use of non-sugar sweeteners for weight control, and released guidelines warning of “potential undesirable effects” from their long-term use, such as an increased risk of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular diseases.

articles.title: Delhi Police release video of informing Dipke of grandmother’s death in detention - watch
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Delhi Police on Sunday released a video showing officers informing Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke about his grandmother’s
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Delhi Police on Sunday released a video showing officers informing Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke about his grandmother’s death while he was in detention in the national capital. Deputy Commissioner of Police Neha Yadav said Dipke was offered assistance to travel to his hometown for the last rites.DCP Neha Yadav said officers approached Dipke as soon as they received information about his grandmother’s demise and offered help with flights, phone calls and other arrangements but the CJP founder declined.“As soon as the Delhi Police received information about the passing away of Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) Founder Abhijeet Dipke's grandmother, officers approached him to convey this sad news and offered all possible assistance. They sensitively asked if he needed help with flights, phone calls, or anything else. They repeatedly asked if he wished to speak to his parents, but he declined,” DCP Yadav said.The video release came after Dipke’s mother, Anita Dipke, accused Delhi Police of lying about informing her son of the death, saying the family had been unable to contact him and had put the last rites on hold until he could return.Responding to Dipke's mother, Delhi Police clarified that Dipke was informed about the death and the scheduled funeral time, and was offered assistance to facilitate his travel to his hometown on humanitarian grounds. However, the police said he declined the offer.Dipke’s paternal grandmother, Savitribai Shankarrao Dipke, 85, died at her home in Santuk Pimpri village in Maharashtra’s Hingoli district at 11.30am on Saturday following a prolonged illness and age-related ailments. Her last rites were scheduled for 10am on Sunday.Police on why Dipke was detainedDipke, along with CJP co-convenor Saurav Das and leader Ashutosh Ranka, was detained on October 10 after arriving in Delhi from Mumbai ahead of the party’s proposed protest at Jantar Mantar demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.DCP Yadav said permission for the proposed sit-in at Janpath was denied because of the party’s alleged failure to follow prescribed procedures, its past conduct and the prevailing security situation. She also cited restrictions imposed under Section 133 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) in several areas."Regarding CJP, their past conduct showed a failure to adhere to previously given undertakings and local directives. When permission was granted previously, they did not abide by the law; the crowd they mobilized engaged in heavy stone-pelting, arson, and violence, causing significant damage to public property," she said."Permission for the proposed sit-in protest at Janpath was denied due to the failure to follow prescribed procedures, a history of non-compliance with laws and guidelines, and the prevailing security and law-and-order situation," she added.The three CJP leaders were subsequently released after being produced before an Executive Magistrate at Delhi Cantt Police Station, subject to an undertaking to maintain public order for one year, according to the party’s legal affairs head, Ratna Singh.Following his release, Dipke reiterated that the party would continue its protests. “Haven’t signed any bond that says we won’t protest. We will hit the streets again,” he said in a post on X on Sunday.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
